column2: Having said this, the best of the Bharatas, the mighty one, raised his mace and stood up for battle, challenging as Shakra challenged Vritra.
Seeing the mighty son of Dhritarashtra alone, like an elephant separated from its herd, the Pandavas rejoiced.
Seeing him with mace raised, like Kailasa with its peaks, Bhimasena then, O king, spoke to Duryodhana.

Remember the evil deed done to us by King Dhritarashtra and by you, what happened at Varanavata,
mahabharata:9:32.38	and Draupadi tormented in the midst of the assembly in her season, and the king (Yudhishthira) won at dice by Shakuni's crafty plan.
mahabharata:9:32.39	And whatever other sins you committed, wicked one, against the blameless Parthas—behold the great fruit of them now.
mahabharata:9:32.40	Because of you the greatly renowned son of Ganga, best of the Bharatas, grandsire of us all, lies on a bed of arrows.
mahabharata:9:32.41	Drona is slain, and Karna, and the valiant Shalya; and Shakuni, the first author of this enmity, has been slain in battle.
mahabharata:9:32.42	Your brothers, heroes, are slain, and your sons with their soldiers, and kings, heroes who never turned back in battle.
mahabharata:9:32.43	These and many other bulls among kshatriyas are slain, and the sinful Pratikamin who tormented Draupadi is slain.
mahabharata:9:32.44	You alone remain, destroyer of the family, vilest of men; I shall slay you too today with my mace, without doubt.
mahabharata:9:32.45	Today I shall destroy all your pride in battle, O king, your vast hope of kingship and your wrongs against the Pandavas.
[Duryodhana said:] "Why boast so much? Fight me today. Today I shall remove your eagerness for battle, Vrikodara.
Do you not see me, wicked one, standing in battle, holding a great mace like a peak of the Himalaya?
What foe dares today to conquer me, mace in hand? Even among the gods, fighting fairly, only Purandara (Indra) might.
Do not roar in vain, son of Kunti, like an autumn cloud without water; show your strength in the fight, as much as you have today."
Hearing his words, the Panchalas and Srinjayas, all eager for victory, applauded that speech.
With the sound of clapping the men again gladdened King Duryodhana, like an elephant in rut.
Elephants trumpeted there, horses neighed again and again, and the weapons of the victory-seeking Pandavas blazed.
Then Rama of the palm-banner, the plough-bearer, hearing that the fight between his two pupils had arrived, came there, O king.
Seeing him, the kings, glad, honoured him and said, "Rama, behold the skill of your two pupils in battle."
Then Rama, seeing Krishna and the Pandava, and Duryodhana the Kaurava standing mace in hand, said:
It is forty-two days since I set out; I departed under Pushya and have come back under Shravana; I wish to see the mace-fight of my two pupils, Madhava.
Then King Yudhishthira embraced the plough-bearer and asked him duly of his welcome and well-being.
The two Krishnas, great archers, also greeted the plough-bearer and embraced him, glad, the renowned ones, as he was dear to them.
The two sons of Madri, heroes, and the five sons of Draupadi stood having greeted the mighty son of Rohini, O king.
Then mighty Bhimasena and your son, lord of men, with their maces raised, likewise honoured his strength.
Welcoming him again and again there, they said to Rama, "Mighty-armed one, behold the battle." So the kings spoke to the great-souled son of Rohini.
Then Rama embraced the Pandavas and the Srinjayas too and asked all the Pandavas of immeasurable might about their welfare; and they too, approaching, asked him if he was well.
The great-minded plough-bearer, honouring all the kshatriyas in turn, and exchanging courteous greetings according to age,
embraced Janardana and Satyaki with love, and having smelled their heads in greeting asked of their welfare.
Those two honoured him duly as their teacher, O king, as Indra and Upendra, glad, honour Brahma, lord of the gods.
Then the son of Dharma said to the son of Rohini, subduer of foes: "Behold, Rama, this great fight of the two brothers, Bharata."
In their midst, the mighty-armed and glorious elder brother of Keshava sat down, highly pleased, honoured by the great chariot-warriors.
In the midst of the kings, clad in blue and white-lustred, he shone like the moon surrounded by hosts of stars in the sky.
Then there came about between the two, your son and Bhima, a tumultuous, hair-raising encounter that was to end the enmity, O king.
[Janamejaya said:] "I shall not give aid to Dhritarashtra's son, Keshava, nor shall I go to the sons of Pandu; I go as I came."
Having said this, Rama, destroyer of foes, departed; you ought to tell, Brahmana, of his return again.
Tell me in detail how Rama came to be present and how he saw the fight; you are skilled, best of men."
[Vaishampayana said:] When the great-souled Pandavas were encamped at Upaplavya, Madhusudana was sent to Dhritarashtra for peace, mighty-armed one, for the welfare of all embodied beings.
Having gone to Hastinapura and met Dhritarashtra, he spoke true and beneficial words, especially so; but the king did not act as advised, as was told to you earlier.
Failing to obtain peace there, Krishna, best of men, the mighty-armed, returned to Upaplavya, lord of men.
Then Krishna, returned and dismissed by Dhritarashtra's side, told the Pandavas, tiger among men, of the failure:
The Kurus, urged by Time, do not follow my words; march out, Pandavas, with me, under Pushya.
Then, as the forces were being divided, the best of the strong, the great-minded son of Rohini, spoke to his brother Krishna:
Let aid be given to them also, mighty-armed Madhusudana. But Krishna did not then do his bidding.
Then the delight of the Yadus, the plough-bearer of great fame, his mind seized by anger, set out on a pilgrimage to the Sarasvati under the constellation Maitra, with all the Yadavas.
Bhoja, subduer of foes, took refuge with Duryodhana, and Vasudeva with Satyaki took the side of the Pandavas.
When the hero, the son of Rohini, had gone under Pushya, Madhusudana, putting the Pandavas in front, advanced against the Kurus.
Going along, standing on the road, Rama said to his messengers, "Ho! Bring from Dvaravati the provisions for the pilgrimage and all the equipment, the fires and the sacrificial priests,
gold and silver, cows, clothes, horses, elephants and chariots, mules, camels and carriages; quickly bring all the paraphernalia for the sake of the tirthas.
Go swiftly against the current of the Sarasvati, and bring priests and hundreds of the best of the twice-born."
Having so instructed his messengers, mighty Baladeva set out on pilgrimage, O king, at the time of the Kurus' destruction, and went to the Sarasvati against the current, from the sea.
Surrounded by priests, friends and other best Brahmanas, by chariots, elephants, horses and messengers, O best of the Bharatas, and by many vehicles drawn by cows, mules and camels,
for the weary, those of tired bodies, the children and the long-lived, vehicles were kept waiting in the regions, O Bharata, and food was provided on every side for the hungry.
Whichever Brahmana in any place wished to eat as he pleased, it was brought to him in that very place, O king.
By command of the son of Rohini, men stationed there made heaps of food and drink on every side.
Costly garments and bedsteads with coverings were provided there as honour for Brahmanas wishing comfort.
Wherever a Brahmana or a kshatriya slept, O Bharata, there everything for him was seen provided.
All people stayed or went at their ease; for one wishing to travel there were vehicles, for the thirsty drinks,
and for the hungry tasty foods, best of the Bharatas; men there brought garments and ornaments.
That road shone, O king, bringing comfort to all, like heaven, O hero, for the men going there.
Ever cheerful, with tasty food and auspicious things, with markets and wares and surrounded by hundreds of people, adorned with various trees and creepers and decked with many jewels,
then the great-souled one, firm in his vow, the delight of the Yadus, the plough-bearer, glad, gave wealth to Brahmanas at the holy tirthas, and sacrificial fees.
He gave to Brahmanas thousands of milch cows, fine-clothed, with horns bound in gold, and horses born in various lands, vehicles and maidservants.
Rama gave to the best of the twice-born jewels, pearls, gems, coral, horned cattle, gold and bright silver, and vessels of iron and copper.
Thus the great-souled one gave abundant wealth at the best of the Sarasvati's tirthas, and in due course the magnanimous one, of unequalled power, came to Kurukshetra.
[Janamejaya said:] "Tell me the origin of the merits of the Sarasvati tirthas, and their fruit, best of the twice-born, and the accomplishment of rites there,
in order, revered one, each of the tirthas in sequence, Brahmana, best of Brahma-knowers; my curiosity is very great."
[Vaishampayana said:] "Hear from me, O king, the account of the tirthas and the origin of their merits, holy and complete, O king of kings.
First, great king, the delight of the Yadus, with priests, friends and companies of Brahmanas, came to holy Prabhasa, where the Lord of Stars (the Moon), afflicted by consumption,
freed of the curse and regaining his radiance, lights the whole world, O lord of men. Thus it is the best tirtha on earth, and from his shining (prabhasana) it is called Prabhasa."
[Janamejaya said:] "Why was the revered Soma seized by consumption, and how did the Moon plunge into that best of tirthas?
And how, bathing in it, was the Hare-marked one restored? Tell me all this in detail, great sage."
[Vaishampayana said:] "Lord of men, there were the daughters of Daksha; Daksha gave twenty-seven maidens to Soma.
They were devoted to the conjunctions of the stars, and to reckoning them, Bharata, the auspicious wives of Soma, O king of kings.
All those large-eyed ones were unmatched on earth in beauty, but Rohini surpassed them in the wealth of her form.
So the revered Moon took delight in her; she was dear to his heart, and therefore he always enjoyed her.
Of old, O king of kings, Soma dwelt long with Rohini; then the other stars of the great one grew angry.
Going to their father the Prajapati, they said without lassitude, 'Soma does not dwell with us; he always serves Rohini.
Therefore, lord of creatures, we shall all together live near you, eating moderately and devoted to austerities.'
Hearing their words, Daksha said to Soma, 'Behave equally toward your wives, lest great unrighteousness touch you.'
And Daksha said to them all, 'Go to Soma; by my command the Moon will dwell equally with all.'
Sent away, they went then to the house of the cool-rayed one; yet the revered Soma, O lord of the earth, again dwelt only with Rohini, delighting in her again and again.
Then they all together spoke again to their father: 'Devoted to serving you, we shall live in your hermitage; Soma does not dwell with us, he has not done your bidding.'
Hearing their words, Daksha said to Soma, 'Behave equally toward your wives, or I shall curse you, radiant one.'
Disregarding Daksha's word, the revered Moon dwelt with Rohini, and the others, enraged, again
went to their father, bowing their heads, and said: 'Soma does not dwell with us; therefore be our refuge.
Revered one, the Moon always dwells with Rohini alone; therefore save us all, that Soma may enter into us.'
Hearing this, the revered one, angry, lord of the earth, in wrath sent consumption against Soma, and it entered the Lord of Stars.
Overcome by consumption, the Moon waned day by day, and made effort, O king, to be freed from the consumption.
Though he performed various sacrifices, great king, the Maker of Night was not freed from the curse and went toward decay.
With Soma waning, the herbs were not born; all were tasteless of flavour and wholly robbed of potency.
With the decay of herbs came decay of living beings; all creatures grew thin as the Maker of Night waned.
Then the gods assembled and said to Soma, lord of the earth, 'Why does your form not shine thus?
Tell us the whole cause by which you have this great fear; having heard it from you, we shall act.'
Thus addressed, the Hare-marked one told them all of the curse and its cause, and of the consumption, as regards himself.
Hearing his words, the gods went to Daksha and said, 'Be gracious, revered one, to Soma; let this curse be withdrawn.
This Moon is wasted; only a little remains visible; and with his decay, lord of gods, creatures have gone to decay.
Creepers, herbs and the various seeds too; so, teacher of the world, you ought to show grace to us.'
Thus addressed, the Prajapati reflected and said: 'This word of mine cannot be turned aside otherwise; but by some means, great ones, it will be turned back.
Let the Moon behave equally to all his wives always; and plunging into the best tirtha of the Sarasvati, the Hare-marked one will wax again, gods; that word of mine is true.
For half the month Soma will ever wane, and for half the month wax; this word of mine is true.'
Then, by the sage's command, Soma went to the Sarasvati, to Prabhasa, the supreme tirtha of the Sarasvati.
On the new-moon day the greatly radiant one, plunging there, lit up the worlds and regained his coolness of ray.
And all the gods, O king of kings, having reached abundant Prabhasa, together with Soma, came before Daksha.
Then the Prajapati dismissed all the gods, and, pleased, the revered one spoke again to Soma:
'Do not disdain women, son, nor ever Brahmanas; go, always attentive, and do my bidding.'
Dismissed, great king, he went to his own abode, and creatures, glad, ate as before.
All this I have told you—how the Maker of Night was cursed and how Prabhasa became the best of tirthas.
On each new-moon day, great king, the Hare-marked, glorious one, bathing in the supreme tirtha Prabhasa, is restored.
Hence people know it as Prabhasa, O lord of the earth, for the Moon obtained supreme radiance (prabha) by plunging in it.
Then the mighty Achyuta (Balarama) went to Chamasodbheda, which people call Chamasodbheda.
There the plough-bearer gave excellent gifts, spent one night, and bathed duly.
Then the elder brother of Keshava quickly went to Udapana, and there, obtaining first a blessing, gained great fruit.
Through the moistness of the herbs and the earth, Janamejaya, the perfected know of the Sarasvati, O king of kings, even when lost."
There, giving much wealth and honouring Brahmanas, and bathing there, the club-bearer (Balarama) was delighted.
There the great ascetic Trita was devoted to dharma; dwelling in a well, that great soul drank Soma.
Leaving him there, his two brothers went home; then Trita, best of Brahmanas, cursed them both.
[Janamejaya said:] "How, Brahmana, was there a well, and how did the great ascetic, best of the twice-born, fall in and get abandoned by his brothers?
And how did the two brothers leave him in the well and go home? Tell me this, Brahmana, if you think it fit to hear."
[Vaishampayana said:] "In the former age, O king, there were three brothers, sages: Ekata, Dvita and Trita, radiant as the sun.
All were equal to Prajapatis, with offspring, conquerors of Brahma's world by austerity, expounders of the Veda.
Pleased by their austerity, restraint and self-control, their father Gautama, ever devoted to dharma, was constantly gratified.
After a long time, having received their affection, the revered one went to a place befitting himself.
The kings who had been that great soul's patrons, when he had gone to heaven, honoured his sons.
By their deeds and study, O king, Trita attained pre-eminence, just as his father had.
All the greatly fortunate sages of auspicious marks honoured him, the greatly fortunate, for his learning.
Once, O king, the brothers Ekata and Dvita set their minds on a sacrifice, and particularly on wealth.
This thought came to them, taking Trita, scorcher of foes: 'Taking all our patrons and accepting animals,
let us, glad, drink Soma, having obtained a sacrifice of great fruit.' And the three brothers did so, great king.
Thus they went round to all their patrons for animals, performed sacrifices for them, and having obtained patrons and very many animals,
accepting by that priestly work according to rule, those great sages came to the eastern region.
Trita, great king, walked in front of them, glad, while Ekata and Dvita behind drove the animals.
Seeing the great herd of animals, they were troubled: 'How can these cattle be ours without Trita?'
Speaking together, Ekata and Dvita, hear, lord of men, what those sinful ones said to one another.
'Trita is skilled in sacrifices, Trita is versed in the Vedas; he will get many other cattle.
So let the two of us go together driving the cows; let Trita go as he likes, without us.'
As they were travelling at night, a wolf appeared on the way, and nearby on the bank of the Sarasvati there was a great well.
Then Trita, seeing the wolf standing ahead on the road, fled from fear and fell into that well, deep, most dreadful, terrifying to all beings.
Then the greatly fortunate Trita, best of sages, in the well, cried out in distress, and the two sages heard him.
Knowing him fallen into the well, the brothers Ekata and Dvita, from fear of the wolf and greed, abandoned him and went on.
Abandoned by his two brothers, greedy for animals, the great ascetic was in the waterless well, O great king, covered with dust.
Trita, seeing himself sunk in the well covered with creepers and grass, O best of the Bharatas, like a sinner in hell,
reflected in his wisdom, afraid of death as one who had not drunk Soma: 'How shall I, staying here, drink Soma?'
Thus reflecting, the great ascetic in that well saw a creeper hanging there by chance.
Then in that dust-filled well the sage thought of water, and imagined fires, himself as the hotri priest.
Then, the great ascetic imagining that creeper to be Soma, mentally thinking of the Rik, Yajus and Saman verses, made pebbles into pressing-stones and performed the pressing, O king.
He made ghee and water, and the shares of the dwellers in heaven, and having pressed the Soma he made a tumultuous sound.
That sound of Trita's entered heaven, O king, and he accomplished that sacrifice as prescribed by the expounders of the Veda.
While the sacrifice of the great-souled Trita proceeded, all heaven was agitated and did not understand the cause.
Then Brihaspati heard that tumultuous noise, and hearing it, the priest of the gods said to all the gods:
'Trita's sacrifice is going on; let us go there, gods, for that great ascetic, angry, might create other gods.'
Hearing his words, all the gods together went to where Trita's sacrifice was proceeding.
Going there, the gods came to the well where Trita was, and saw that great soul initiated in the sacrificial rites.
Seeing that great soul endowed with supreme splendour, they said to the greatly fortunate one, 'We have come seeking our shares.'
Then the sage said to the gods, 'See me, dwellers in heaven, sunk in this terrifying well, my senses lost.'
Then Trita, great king, gave them their shares duly, with mantras, and they were pleased.
Then the dwellers in heaven, having received their shares duly, pleased at heart, gave him boons of whatever he desired in his mind.
He chose this boon from the gods: 'You should rescue me from here; and whoever bathes in this well should gain the state of a Soma-drinker.'
Thereupon the Sarasvati, full of waves, rose up there, O king, and lifted by her Trita stood, honouring the dwellers in heaven.
Saying "So be it," the gods went as they had come, O king, and Trita too, pleased, went to his own dwelling.
Angry, he met those two sages, his brothers, and the great ascetic spoke harshly and cursed them.
'Because you, greedy for animals, abandoned me and ran away, therefore in form you shall roam about among fanged beasts.
You shall be so by my curse for this sinful deed, and your offspring shall be langurs, bears and monkeys.'
At these words of his, O lord of men, in a moment they were seen so transformed by the word of the truth-speaker.
There too the one of immeasurable valour, the plough-bearer, touched the water, gave gifts of various kinds, and honoured Brahmanas.
Seeing that well and praising it again and again, the undespondent one went to the river and reached Vinashana.
Because that Sarasvati, best of the Bharatas, was lost from hatred, therefore the sages ever call it Vinashana.
Having bathed in that too, mighty Bala went on the Sarasvati's excellent bank to Subhumika.
He saw the loud-voiced, large-bodied owl, tawny-eyed, brown and yellow, with a long beak and claws, swift like Garuda.
Thus consoled by the great-souled Sanjaya, Vidura again spoke with deliberate wisdom, scorcher of foes.
But afterwards I learned, best of Brahmanas, that Karna was my uterine brother and elder, by the word of Pritha, lord.
This being so, I am not at fault, I am not to be killed, I am not guilty; if you think there is guilt in a concurrence, then it may be so.
All the doctrines of liberation have been heard by you as they truly are, and your doubts born of desire have been cut by me repeatedly.
While the great-souled Pandavas lived in righteous conduct, King Dhritarashtra, son of Ambika, was pleased.
The blazing fire turned leftward, dark-blue and red, emitting flames of madder hue in separate streams.
The discus-jewel that dwelt in the great-souled Krishna has gone, and will again come to his hand in time.
[The gods said:] "If you have faith in that, son, go there without delay; we are at your service by the command of the king of the gods."
